title: Tell Your Students to Quit Something
author: How to Teach With AI
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 31, 2026
summary: Writing in response to the University of Michigan's decision to shield first-semester grades starting in fall 2027, the author argues that grade-covering policies miss the real driver of student distress: sheer volume of commitments. The piece contends that well-meaning parents, counselors, and advisors nudge students into stacking majors, minors, clubs, jobs, and internships until no time remains for rest or genuine depth, and that employers do not reward this breadth since a transcript cannot demonstrate what a student can actually do. The author's proposed fix is subtraction rather than grade insurance, and lays out a specific 20-minute advising conversation built around an inventory of commitments, a payoff question for each item, and a trade-off question that surfaces which activities are undermining the others. The piece closes with a five-step "subtraction audit" homework assignment that pushes students toward keeping only three commitments: one for depth, one for money if needed, and one purely for love.
points: Grade-shielding policies like Michigan's cannot fix student overload because the crushing factor is volume of commitments, not fear of a bad grade appearing on a transcript.
The author frames the stacking pattern as "credential stacking" -- students collecting resume lines nobody will read at the cost of the hours that could produce real, demonstrable work.
Employers do not hire the second major or minor; they hire proof of what a student can do, which comes from depth and repetition rather than breadth.

The advising fix is a structured questioning sequence (inventory, payoff question, trade-off question) that lets an overcommitted student talk themselves into cutting their own list rather than being told to quit.

The five-step subtraction audit forces students to keep only three commitments -- a depth pursuit, a money pursuit if necessary, and a joy pursuit -- and to protect unscheduled time as load-bearing rest.
quotes: My whole argument, for the skimmers: the pressure crushing our students is volume, and grade policy can't touch volume. Students are coached by parents, counselors, advisors, and most of us to stack majors, minors, clubs, titles, jobs, and internships until there's no room left to think, explore, play, and relax. The fix is subtraction.
I'll call the pattern what it is: credential stacking. Students collecting lines for a resume nobody will read, paid for with the hours that could have built something worth reading about.
They can't look at a transcript and know what a student can do. A letter grade is a claim about compliance with a course, and they already suspect the course content is years out of date.

Skills don't come from breadth. They come from repetitions, from going deep on one thing long enough to produce work our students can put in front of someone. A student sprinting between four obligations a day never gets the repetitions.

Ask the trade question. Hours are finite, so every item on the list is quietly taxing the others. "Which of these is making the others worse?" They know, they've just never been asked to say it out loud.

Arm them with the payoff question you asked in your office. Parents can argue with a preference. They have a harder time arguing with "this path produces work I can show a hiring manager, and the other one produces a heavier transcript.
A covered grade protects a student from one bad October. A shorter list gives them back their four years.
